newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe down in poll after tax-cutting package.
newsitem.headline: Juppe down in poll after tax-cutting package.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's popularity plummeted in September following a widely-criticised tax-cutting package, an opinion poll showed on Tuesday.
The BVA poll for the weekly Paris-Match said 63 percent had a bad opinion of the conservative premier, up from 55 percent in August and his worst score since February.
Those with a good opinion fell to 31 percent from 37 percent.
The poll also showed that 54 percent thought poorly of President Jacques Chirac, against 46 percent a month previously. Forty percent had a good opinion against 46 percent in August.

Juppe said earlier this month that he would cut income taxes by 75 billion francs ($14.7 billion) over five years, with 25 billion francs applying in 1997 on 1996 income, in a bid to restore confidence and boost consumer spending to help a stagnating economy.
But income tax cuts for the better off were offset by hikes in other taxes that hit everyone.
Critics called it a transparent political ploy for votes in a 1998 general election, a gift to the rich at the expense of the poor and a contradiction with efforts to cut the budget deficit.
The poll interviewed 931 people between September 19-21.
A separate CSA survey for the weekly La Vie found that Chirac's popularity had slightly increased while that of Juppe was stagnating at its lowest level since he took power last year.
The poll showed that 44 percent of the French trusted the head of state to tackle issues, against 41 percent a month previously. Thirty-eight percent had no confidence in him.
Thirty-three percent expressed confidence in Juppe, the same as last month. Fifty-eight percent had no confidence in him, against 56 percent a month ago.
The survey was carried out on September 16 and 17 and interviewed 1,000 people.
